tasks.title: Hello, world!
tasks.statement:
Write a program that prints a single line: «Hello, world!»

Expected output:
«Hello, world!»
tasks.hint: Inside fn main() call println!("…"); do not forget the semicolon at the end.

tasks.title: Two lines
tasks.statement:
Print two lines: first «My name is Rust», then «I am already more than ten years old».

Expected output:
«My name is Rust
I am already more than ten years old»
tasks.hint: Each println! call prints a line and ends it. Two calls — two lines.

tasks.title: print! without a newline
tasks.statement:
Using three calls of print! (not println!), print on one line «One, two, three!», and then make one call of println!() that only ends the line.

Expected output:
«One, two, three!»
tasks.hint: print!("…") does not add a newline; an empty println!() ends the line.

tasks.title: Substituting values
tasks.statement:
Print the equation 2 + 3 = 5, passing the numbers 2, 3 and 5 as arguments of println! (use three pairs of {} in the string).

Expected output:
2 + 3 = 5
tasks.hint: println!("{} + {} = {}", 2, 3, 5); — the values are substituted left to right.

tasks.title: An expression right in the argument
tasks.statement:
Print the line «Sum: 12», but let the program compute the number 12: pass the expression 5 + 7 to println!.

Expected output:
«Sum: 12»
tasks.hint: Any expression can be an argument of println!: println!("Sum: {}", 5 + 7);

tasks.title: Names inside the braces
tasks.statement:
Declare two variables: `let name = "Anya"; let age = 30;` and print «Anya, 30 years», inserting them right into the string: {name} and {age} (no arguments after the string).

Expected output:
«Anya, 30 years»
tasks.hint: If you write a variable name inside the braces, println! takes its value: {name}.

tasks.title: Real curly braces
tasks.hint: To print one curly brace, write two in a row: {{ and }}.

tasks.title: Quotes and the backslash
tasks.statement:
Print two lines. The first: «He said: "hello"» (with double quotes inside). The second: C:\temp\new (with backslashes).

Expected output:
«He said: "hello"»
C:\temp\new
tasks.hint: Inside a string a quote is written as \" and a backslash as \\.

tasks.title: Tab
tasks.statement:
Print a table of two lines where the columns are separated by the tab character \t: «Name<tab>Age» and «Anya<tab>30».

Expected output:
«Name	Age»
«Anya	30»
tasks.hint: \t inside a string is one tab character.

tasks.title: Business card
tasks.statement:
Print a business card of four lines (the output is shown below; note the frame made of the characters + - |).

Expected output:
+----------------+
«| Anya Petrov    |
| Rust-learner   |»
+----------------+
tasks.hint: Each line of the card is a separate println!; the spaces inside the quotes matter.

tasks.title: A cat from characters
tasks.statement:
Draw a cat in four lines (the exact look is in the expected output below).

Expected output:
 /\_/\
( o.o )
 > ^ <
«meow!»
tasks.hint: A backslash in a string is written as \\ — otherwise it starts an escape sequence.

tasks.title: A receipt with calculations
tasks.statement:
Print a receipt: «Bread: 40», «Milk: 95», «Cheese: 310» and the total line «Total: 445». Do not type the total by hand — compute it with the expression 40 + 95 + 310 right inside println!.

Expected output:
«Bread: 40
Milk: 95
Cheese: 310
Total: 445»

tasks.title: 3×3 multiplication table
tasks.statement:
Print a 3×3 multiplication table: three lines, each with three numbers separated by spaces (the products i·j). Compute the products in the arguments of println!, do not type the finished numbers.

Expected output:
1 2 3
2 4 6
3 6 9
tasks.hint: println!("{} {} {}", 1 * 1, 1 * 2, 1 * 3); — and so on for three lines.

tasks.title: Number bases
tasks.statement:
Print the number 42 in four ways on one line separated by spaces: decimal ({}), binary ({:b}), hexadecimal ({:x}) and octal ({:o}).

Expected output:
42 101010 2a 52
tasks.hint: The format goes after the colon inside the braces: b — binary, x — hexadecimal, o — octal.

tasks.title: Aligning by width
tasks.statement:
Print the number 42 in three ways, each in square brackets on its own line: right-aligned in five positions [   42], left-aligned [42   ] and zero-padded [00042]. Use {:>5}, {:<5} and {:05}.

Expected output:
[   42]
[42   ]
[00042]
tasks.hint: >5 — right-aligned, <5 — left-aligned, 05 — pad with zeros to five positions.

tasks.title: How many decimal places
tasks.statement:
Print the number 3.14159 with two decimal places (3.14), and the number 2.0 / 3.0 with three (0.667), each on its own line. The formats are {:.2} and {:.3}.

Expected output:
3.14
0.667
tasks.hint: {:.2} — two decimal places; rounding is done automatically.

tasks.title: Debug output {:?}
tasks.statement:
Print on one line separated by spaces using {:?}: the string "text", the number 5, the character 'a' and the tuple (1, 2.5, true). The {:?} format shows values the way they look in code (with the string in quotes).

Expected output:
"text" 5 'a' (1, 2.5, true)
tasks.hint: {:?} works for almost any value — handy for debugging.

tasks.title: Raw string
tasks.statement:
Print the path C:\Users\anna\docs with a single raw string r"…" (in such a string backslashes do not need to be doubled).

Expected output:
C:\Users\anna\docs
tasks.hint: r"…" is a raw string: it has no escape sequences inside. You can pass it as an argument for {}.

tasks.title: Russian and Unicode
tasks.statement:
Print two lines: «Раст любит Unicode» and «Краб 🦀 говорит привет».

Expected output:
«Раст любит Unicode
Краб 🦀 говорит привет»
tasks.hint: Strings in Rust are UTF-8, so Russian letters and emoji can be written right inside the quotes.

tasks.title: A string of several lines
tasks.statement:
With a single call of println!, print three lines: «First», «Second», «Third». To do this, put two newline characters \n into the string (or write the string over several lines of code).

Expected output:
«First
Second
Third»
tasks.hint: \n inside a string is a newline; println! adds one more at the very end.

tasks.title: The five arithmetic operations
tasks.statement:
Print five lines with operations on the integers 7 and 3: «7 + 3 = 10», «7 - 3 = 4», «7 * 3 = 21», «7 / 3 = 2» (integer division) and «7 % 3 = 1» (remainder). Compute the results in the program.

Expected output:
7 + 3 = 10
7 - 3 = 4
7 * 3 = 21
7 / 3 = 2
7 % 3 = 1
tasks.hint: Integers divide with truncation: 7 / 3 gives 2, and the remainder is 7 % 3.

tasks.title: Floating-point numbers
tasks.statement:
Print three lines: 7.0 / 3.0 with three decimal places, 2.5 * 4.0 with one, and 10.0 - 0.1 with two (only the results, one number per line).

Expected output:
2.333
10.0
9.90
tasks.hint: Floating-point literals are written with a dot: 7.0, not 7.

tasks.title: Seconds in a day
tasks.statement:
Print the line «A day has 86400 seconds», computing the number with the expression 24 * 60 * 60 inside println!.

Expected output:
«A day has 86400 seconds»
tasks.hint: println!("A day has {} seconds", 24 * 60 * 60);

tasks.title: Area of a circle
tasks.statement:
The area of a circle with radius 5 is 3.14159 · 5 · 5. Print «Area: 78.54» (two decimal places), computing the number in the program.

Expected output:
«Area: 78.54»
tasks.hint: Fractional numbers in the expression use a dot: 3.14159 * 5.0 * 5.0; format {:.2}.

tasks.title: Celsius and Fahrenheit
tasks.statement:
Print «100°C = 212°F», computing 212 with the formula 100.0 * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 (print the number with no decimal places: format {:.0}).

Expected output:
100°C = 212°F
tasks.hint: {:.0} rounds to an integer; remember that floating-point literals are written with a dot.

tasks.title: True and false
tasks.statement:
Print on one line separated by spaces the results of the comparisons 5 > 3, 2 + 2 == 5 and 4 <= 4 (you get: true false true).

Expected output:
true false true
tasks.hint: A comparison is an expression of type bool; println! prints it as true or false.

tasks.title: A character and its number
tasks.statement:
Print the character 'R' and its numeric Unicode code using as: «R 82». For this use the expression 'R' as u32.

Expected output:
R 82
tasks.hint: as u32 turns a char into a number — its code.

tasks.title: Progress bar
tasks.statement:
Print a progress bar of ten characters: five hash signs and five hyphens in square brackets, then a space and 50%.

Expected output:
[#####-----] 50%
tasks.hint: The percent sign in println! is printed as is: you do not need to escape the % character in the format.

tasks.title: Daily schedule
tasks.statement:
Print a schedule of five lines in the format «time<tab>activity»: 08:00 «exercise», 09:00 «work», 13:00 «lunch», 18:00 «walk», 22:00 «sleep».

Expected output:
«08:00	exercise»
«09:00	work»
«13:00	lunch»
«18:00	walk»
«22:00	sleep»
tasks.hint: Separate the time and the activity with the \t character.

tasks.title: Comments are not printed
tasks.statement:
The program must print exactly two lines: «Visible» and «Also visible». Between the two println! calls add two comments: a line comment (// …) with any text and a block comment (/* … */) containing the fragment `println!("should not be visible");` — it must not run.

Expected output:
«Visible
Also visible»
tasks.hint: Everything after // to the end of the line and inside /* … */ is a comment; the compiler skips it.
